takeaway: Ananke transparently survives a user-space file-system process crash by replaying a protected operation log against durable state while a preinitialized replacement process takes over.
background: A microkernel-style file system runs in a user process, so its failure need not crash applications or the host OS. Restarting it is insufficient, however: applications may depend on dirty pages, open descriptors, offsets, and completed operations that ordinary whole-system crash recovery never made durable.
villain: Forcing every operation to storage closes this state gap but destroys common-case performance; replaying every call naively can duplicate already durable effects or violate changed preconditions. Recovery must also distrust the failed process's memory and reestablish device and IPC connections quickly.
approach: Ananke records state-changing calls and their affected descriptors/inodes in replicated, checksummed per-core p-logs. Its Act–Ignore–Modify algorithm combines log status with on-disk recovery to replay only the missing effects, rescuing referenced dirty pages. The kernel detects failure and activates a preinitialized replacement process; checksums make semantic-memory corruption fail fast.
impact: The system demonstrates that process-level file-system recovery can be stronger and cheaper than treating every failure as a machine crash. It identifies host coordination and transient state captured at failure time as valuable recovery resources unique to microkernel services.

evaluation.overview: Fault injection covers crashes after and during calls, concurrent applications, and exhaustive corruption of major memory regions. Separate experiments measure application throughput, log/checksum memory, garbage-collection tradeoffs, and restart latency.
evaluation.implemented: Approximately 4,000 lines added to the open-source uFS user-space file system, including p-logs, AIM replay, memory checksums, page rescue, and kernel-coordinated speculative restart.
evaluation.setting: A 64-core AMD 2.80 GHz server with 256 GB RAM and a Samsung PM173X NVMe SSD; workloads include GNU sort/copy/unzip, SQLite, LevelDB, YCSB, and injected fail-stop or memory-corruption faults.

results.text: Across more than 30,000 injected p-crash points in five applications, Ananke completes with the expected result and data; 300 additional multi-application crash points also recover correctly.
Fully protected Ananke adds about 7% overhead for its two most write-intensive workloads and below 2% for the others, whereas synchronous persistence makes workloads as much as 6× slower.
Recovery remains below 400 ms in the tested write-intensive workloads because speculative initialization overlaps the roughly 2.9-second device-reconnection setup.

limitations: Ananke assumes correct logging code, an intact recovery stack, successful rescue of referenced pages, and application-level handling of user-data corruption. It does not protect the application–file-system message ring. Nine injected stack/heap corruptions prevented complete data rescue in the current signal-handler implementation, and corruption of both p-log replicas aborts recovery.
phd_group_signal: The paper separates process-crash and system-crash semantics, then supports its recovery invariants with tens of thousands of precisely placed failures and memory corruptions. It models strong systems work that combines a clear fault model, mechanism design, adversarial testing, and common-path cost accounting.

claims.text: AIM classifies each logged operation as Act, Ignore, or Modify so replay reconstructs only transient effects absent from the recovered on-disk state.
Recovery trusts only the replicated, checksummed p-log and explicitly rescued pages; it discards other failed-process memory and rebuilds file-system state from disk.
